title: Thermal insulation
aim: To investigate how the type of insulating material wrapped around a beaker of hot water affects how quickly the water cools, and how the thickness (number of layers) of insulation affects the temperature drop.
background: Hot water in a beaker cools because energy is transferred from the water to the cooler surroundings. Energy is conducted through the glass, the surface of the water and the air above it loses energy by convection and evaporation, and the beaker also emits infrared radiation. The rate of cooling depends on how big the temperature difference between the water and the surroundings is, so hot water cools quickly at first and more slowly as it approaches room temperature.

Thermal insulators have a low thermal conductivity, so they reduce the rate of energy transfer by conduction. Many good insulators, such as cotton wool, bubble wrap and wool, trap pockets of air. Air is a very poor conductor, and because it is trapped it cannot move to set up convection currents.

In this practical identical beakers of hot water are wrapped in different materials, or in different numbers of layers of the same material, and the temperature is measured at regular intervals. A cooling curve (temperature against time) is plotted for each beaker. The best insulator gives the smallest temperature drop over the same time and the shallowest cooling curve.

Thicker insulation (more layers) reduces the rate of energy transfer further. In a house, loft insulation, cavity wall insulation and double glazing use the same idea to reduce the rate of cooling and so reduce heating bills.
hypothesis: The beaker wrapped in the material that traps the most air (cotton wool) will cool most slowly, and increasing the number of layers of insulation will reduce the temperature drop in 15 minutes.

variables.independent: Type of insulating material (none, newspaper, bubble wrap, cotton wool), or the number of layers of newspaper in the second part.
variables.dependent: Temperature of the water (°C) at 3 minute intervals, used to find the temperature drop in 15 minutes.
control: Size, shape and material of the beaker
Same cardboard lid on each beaker
Room temperature and position (away from draughts and radiators)

equipment: Insulating materials: newspaper, bubble wrap, cotton wool
Cardboard lids with a hole for the thermometer
Elastic bands or sticky tape to hold the insulation in place
method: Wrap each beaker in a different insulating material, using the same thickness of each and holding it in place with elastic bands. Leave one beaker unwrapped as a control.
Boil water in a kettle and allow it to cool slightly. Use a measuring cylinder to pour 200 cm³ of hot water into the first beaker.
Place a cardboard lid on the beaker and push a thermometer through the hole so that its bulb is in the water but not touching the glass.
When the temperature falls to 80 °C, start the stopclock and record the temperature.
Record the temperature of the water every 3 minutes for 15 minutes.

Repeat for each of the other beakers, using 200 cm³ of hot water and starting the stopclock at 80 °C each time. All beakers can be set up at the same time if there are enough thermometers and stopclocks.
Calculate the temperature drop in 15 minutes for each material.
Plot a cooling curve (temperature on the y-axis, time on the x-axis) for each beaker on the same axes.
To investigate thickness, repeat the experiment with one beaker wrapped in 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and then 5 layers of newspaper, recording the temperature drop in 15 minutes each time.
Repeat each test and calculate a mean temperature drop for each material or number of layers.

safety.risk: Scalding the skin if the water is spilled or splashes.
safety.precaution: Pour carefully into beakers standing on a heatproof mat, do not carry beakers of hot water around the room, and cool any burn under cold running water.

safety.risk: Cuts if glass breaks, especially when wrapping the beaker or pushing the thermometer through the lid.
safety.precaution: Wrap beakers before adding hot water, push the thermometer gently through a hole that is big enough, and stop thermometers rolling off the bench.

safety.hazard: Kettle and mains electricity near water
safety.precaution: Keep the kettle and its lead away from the edge of the bench and from spilled water, and dry hands before using it.

results.notes: Room temperature was 20 °C. Temperature drops in 15 minutes: no insulation 24.5 °C, newspaper 19.5 °C, bubble wrap 15.0 °C, cotton wool 12.0 °C. Plot a cooling curve for each material on the same axes, with time on the x-axis and temperature on the y-axis, and draw a smooth curve through each set of points. In the thickness investigation with newspaper, the mean temperature drops in 15 minutes were: 0 layers 24.5 °C, 1 layer 20.5 °C, 2 layers 17.5 °C, 3 layers 15.5 °C, 4 layers 14.0 °C, 5 layers 12.5 °C.

analysis: All the beakers cooled, but the unwrapped beaker cooled fastest (24.5 °C drop in 15 minutes) and the beaker wrapped in cotton wool cooled slowest (12.0 °C drop). Cotton wool was the best insulator, followed by bubble wrap and then newspaper.

Each cooling curve is steepest at the start and gets less steep with time. This is because the rate of energy transfer depends on the temperature difference between the water and the room; as the water cools, the difference gets smaller, so it cools more slowly.
Cotton wool and bubble wrap trap a lot of air. Air is a poor conductor and the trapped air cannot form convection currents, so the rate of energy transfer from the water is reduced.

More layers of newspaper gave a smaller temperature drop, but each extra layer made less difference than the one before (a drop of 4.0 °C for the first layer, but only 1.5 °C for the fifth). Increasing the thickness of insulation reduces the rate of cooling, but with diminishing returns.

The mean rate of cooling over 15 minutes can be calculated as temperature drop ÷ time. For example, for cotton wool it is 12.0 ÷ 15 = 0.8 °C per minute, and for no insulation it is 24.5 ÷ 15 ≈ 1.6 °C per minute.

errors.error: The starting temperatures were not exactly the same, which affects the rate of cooling because hotter water cools faster.
errors.improvement: Start the stopclock only when each beaker has cooled to exactly 80 °C.

errors.error: Different thicknesses of the different materials were used, so the test was not fair.
errors.improvement: Use the same thickness of each material, measured with a ruler, and wrap it the same way including the base.

errors.error: Thermometer read at an angle (parallax) or with a resolution of only 1 °C.
errors.improvement: Read at eye level, or use temperature probes and a data logger that record to 0.1 °C at exactly the right times.

errors.error: Draughts or nearby heaters change the rate of cooling of some beakers.
errors.improvement: Place all beakers together in the same part of the room, away from windows, doors and radiators.

errors.error: Readings from a single test may be affected by random errors.
errors.improvement: Repeat each test and calculate a mean temperature drop, identifying and ignoring anomalous results.

examTips: Learn the control variables: same volume and starting temperature of water, same beaker, same lid, same thickness of each material, same time and same room conditions.
When comparing materials, compare the temperature drop over the same time, or the gradient of the cooling curves. A shallower curve means a better insulator.
Explain why good insulators work: they have a low thermal conductivity and many trap air, which is a poor conductor and cannot move to form convection currents.
Cooling curves get less steep over time because the temperature difference between the water and the surroundings gets smaller.
A lid reduces energy transfer by evaporation and convection from the water surface; say this if asked why a lid is used.

questions.question: A student investigates which material is the best insulator by wrapping beakers of hot water in different materials. What is the independent variable?
markScheme: 1 mark: type of insulating material
questions.explanation: The student chooses and changes the material, so it is the independent variable. The temperature is measured (dependent) and the volume of water is kept the same (control).

questions.question: Why is a cardboard lid placed on each beaker of hot water in a thermal insulation investigation?
options: To reduce energy transfer from the water surface by convection and evaporation
To make the water cool faster so the experiment is quicker
To stop the thermometer touching the water
To increase the temperature of the water
markScheme: 1 mark: reduces energy transfer by convection / evaporation from the surface
questions.explanation: Much of the energy lost from an open beaker leaves from the water surface. A lid traps a layer of air above the water and reduces evaporation and convection.

questions.question:
The temperature of the water in an unwrapped beaker fell from 80.0 °C to 55.5 °C in 15 minutes.
Calculate the temperature drop.
questions.explanation: Temperature drop = starting temperature − final temperature = 24.5 °C.

questions.question:
Water in a beaker wrapped in cotton wool cooled from 80.0 °C to 68.0 °C in 15 minutes.
Calculate the mean rate of cooling in °C per minute.
markScheme: 1 mark: temperature drop = 12.0 °C
questions.explanation: Mean rate of cooling = temperature drop ÷ time. Dividing the final temperature by the time (68.0 ÷ 15) is a common mistake.

questions.question:
Four beakers of water started at 80.0 °C. After 15 minutes their temperatures were:
No insulation: 55.5 °C
Newspaper: 60.5 °C
Bubble wrap: 65.0 °C
Cotton wool: 68.0 °C
Which material was the best insulator?
markScheme: 1 mark: cotton wool
questions.explanation: The best insulator keeps the water hottest, so it gives the smallest temperature drop (12.0 °C for cotton wool). The unwrapped beaker had the largest drop.

questions.question:
A student compares how well different materials insulate a beaker of hot water.
Give two variables the student should control.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: volume (mass) of water; starting temperature; size or type of beaker; thickness of insulation; same lid; time of cooling; room temperature or position in room
questions.explanation: Each of these affects the rate of cooling, so changing them would make it impossible to tell whether the material caused the difference.

questions.question:
A cooling curve for a beaker of hot water is steep at first and becomes less steep over time.
Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: smaller difference between water and room
markScheme: 1 mark: the temperature difference between the water and the surroundings decreases (as the water cools)
1 mark: so the rate of energy transfer (rate of cooling) decreases
questions.explanation: The rate at which energy is transferred to the surroundings depends on the temperature difference. Near room temperature the water cools very slowly.

questions.question: Explain why cotton wool is a good thermal insulator.
markScheme: 1 mark: it traps (pockets of) air, which is a poor conductor / has low thermal conductivity
1 mark: the trapped air cannot move, so convection is reduced
questions.explanation: Cotton wool itself is a poor conductor, but its main advantage is the air trapped between the fibres. The air cannot circulate, so energy cannot be carried away by convection.

questions.question:
0.150 kg of water cools from 80 °C to 60 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C.
Calculate the energy transferred from the water to the surroundings.
markScheme: 1 mark: 12600 J
questions.explanation: Use the temperature change (20 °C), not either temperature on its own. 0.150 × 4200 = 630, and 630 × 20 = 12600 J.

questions.question:
A beaker of water loses 12600 J of energy to the surroundings in 15 minutes.
Calculate the mean rate of energy transfer from the water.
markScheme: 1 mark: 15 minutes = 900 s
1 mark: power = energy ÷ time = 12600 ÷ 900
1 mark: 14 W
questions.explanation: Rate of energy transfer is power, P = E ÷ t, with time in seconds. Using 15 instead of 900 gives 840 W, which is far too large.

questions.question:
A beaker with no insulation had a temperature drop of 24.5 °C in 15 minutes. The same beaker wrapped in 5 layers of newspaper had a temperature drop of 12.5 °C in 15 minutes.
Calculate the percentage reduction in temperature drop caused by the newspaper. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 49%
questions.explanation: Percentage reduction = (decrease ÷ original value) × 100 = 12.0 ÷ 24.5 × 100 = 48.98%, which is 49% to 2 significant figures. Dividing by 12.5 instead of 24.5 gives 96%, which is wrong.

questions.question:
The mean temperature drops of water in a beaker in 15 minutes with different numbers of layers of newspaper were:
0 layers: 24.5 °C
1 layer: 20.5 °C
2 layers: 17.5 °C
3 layers: 15.5 °C
4 layers: 14.0 °C
5 layers: 12.5 °C
Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: The temperature drop is inversely proportional to the number of layers
Each extra layer reduces the temperature drop by the same amount
More layers reduce the temperature drop, but each extra layer has a smaller effect
Adding layers has no effect after 2 layers
markScheme: 1 mark: more layers reduce the drop, with each additional layer having a smaller effect
questions.explanation: The reductions are 4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.5 and 1.5 °C, so the effect of each layer gets smaller. The drop is not inversely proportional (doubling from 2 to 4 layers does not halve it), and the effect continues after 2 layers.

questions.question: Give one safety precaution a student should take when using water from a kettle to investigate thermal insulation.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one of: stand beakers on a heatproof mat; pour carefully / do not move beakers of hot water; wipe up spills; cool any burn under cold running water
questions.explanation: The main hazard is scalding from hot water, so precautions should reduce the chance of spilling it or reduce harm if it is spilled.

questions.question:
A student uses a thermometer that reads to the nearest 1 °C to record the temperature of cooling water every 3 minutes.
Suggest one improvement to the way temperature is measured and explain why it is better.
markScheme: 1 mark: use a temperature probe and data logger (or a thermometer with a higher resolution)
1 mark: higher resolution (to 0.1 °C) / readings taken automatically at the exact times / no parallax error
questions.explanation: Small temperature drops in well insulated beakers are hard to compare with a resolution of 1 °C. A data logger also records several beakers at exactly the same times.

questions.question:
Describe a method a student could use to investigate how the thickness of insulation around a beaker affects how quickly hot water in the beaker cools.
Include how the student should make the investigation a fair test.
markScheme: Indicative content: wrap a beaker in a number of layers of the same material (for example newspaper); measure a fixed volume of hot water (for example 200 cm³) with a measuring cylinder; pour into the beaker; add a lid; place a thermometer through the lid into the water; start a stopclock when the water reaches a set starting temperature (for example 80 °C); record the temperature at regular intervals (every 3 minutes) for a fixed time (15 minutes); calculate the temperature drop; repeat with different numbers of layers (0 to 5); repeat each and find the mean; control: same volume and starting temperature, same beaker and lid, same material, same room conditions; plot temperature drop against number of layers or cooling curves; safety: heatproof mat, care with hot water

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, detailed method that would give valid results, clearly stating how thickness is varied, what is measured and when, and including several control variables and repeats.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with the main steps (different layers, hot water, temperature measured over time) but with some control variables or detail missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as wrapping beakers and measuring the temperature, without a clear method.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Good answers change only the number of layers, give exact values for volume, starting temperature, interval and total time, and explain how the results will be compared, such as by temperature drop in 15 minutes.
